summary: This experimental document defines two transport modes for Host Identity Protocol signaling messages, which let them travel over encrypted connections created with HIP. This protects the control messages themselves.

eli5.summary: Instead of whispering instructions in the open, the instructions travel in the already locked tunnel.

questions: how to protect hip control messages
subtitle: Two ways to encrypt HIP control messages using the encrypted connection itself.

tldr.problem: Host Identity Protocol sets up encrypted connections for data traffic but continues sending control messages in the clear, leaving signaling exposed to eavesdropping and analysis.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines two encrypted transport modes for HIP signaling: ESP mode sends messages directly over the encrypted connection, while ESP-TCP mode wraps them in TCP for fragmentation support.
tldr.outcome: HIP implementations can now protect their control messages end-to-end, closing a security gap in the protocol without requiring a new base exchange.

today: RFC 6261 is an Experimental RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains one of the extensions to the Host Identity Protocol for encrypted signaling negotiation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) allows two hosts to set up a secure association and create an encrypted connection for data traffic. However, HIP control messages (signaling) traditionally continue to be sent in the clear over plain IP or UDP, even though an encrypted connection already exists between the hosts.

This RFC defines two encrypted signaling transport modes that allow HIP control messages to be sent over the encrypted connection that HIP has already established for data. The benefit is that all signaling traffic, including HIP headers and parameters, is encrypted end-to-end. Two modes are defined to handle different scenarios: ESP mode sends messages directly over the encrypted connection, while ESP-TCP mode uses TCP within the encrypted tunnel, which handles message fragmentation automatically.

The modes are negotiated during the HIP base exchange or later using UPDATE messages, allowing hosts to agree on which transport to use for subsequent signaling.
sections.eli5: After two computers set up a secret tunnel for talking, they can now also use that same tunnel for their control instructions, instead of shouting them in the hallway.

sections.title: Transport Modes Overview
sections.content:
Two encrypted transport modes are defined. The DEFAULT mode continues to use the same unencrypted transport (plain IP or UDP) that was used for the base exchange, maintaining backward compatibility.

In ESP mode, HIP signaling messages are sent directly as data on the encrypted Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) connection. The ESP header's next-header field is set to HIP (protocol number 139). This provides simple, direct encryption of all signaling traffic. However, if HIP messages become very large (for example, when carrying certificates or large data payloads), they may exceed the path's maximum transmission unit and require IP-level fragmentation, which can be inefficient.

In ESP-TCP mode, TCP is established as a connection within the ESP tunnel. The host with the larger HIT (Host Identity Tag) listens for incoming TCP connections, and the other host initiates the connection. Once established, HIP messages are sent reliably over this TCP connection (the ESP header's next-header is set to TCP, protocol 6). This mode handles message fragmentation at the TCP level, making it suitable for large signaling messages. Since TCP provides reliability, HIP messages are not retransmitted; instead, hosts wait for TCP connection failure to detect lost packets.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to use the tunnel: direct mode (like putting mail in the tunnel) and TCP mode (like setting up a mailbox inside the tunnel). TCP is better for big mail.

sections.title: Mode Negotiation
sections.content:
Transport mode negotiation happens using the HIP_TRANSPORT_MODE parameter (type 7680), which is carried in HIP packets and covered by the packet's signature.

During the base exchange, the Responder lists its supported modes in the R1 packet, ordered by preference. The Initiator either selects one of the offered modes (by including it in the I2 packet) or signals that it cannot use any of them (by including an empty parameter). If the Initiator selects a mode the Responder did not offer, the base exchange fails. Once selected, the mode is used for all subsequent signaling until renegotiated or the association ends.

To change transport modes after the base exchange, a host sends an UPDATE packet with a HIP_TRANSPORT_MODE parameter listing the desired modes. The receiving host responds with the mode it selects from the list, or responds with the currently-in-use mode if none of the proposals are acceptable. If a host receives a HIP_TRANSPORT_MODE parameter it cannot process (because it does not support the extension), it simply replies without the parameter; the proposing host can then close the association if local policy requires the new mode.

If mode negotiation fails, hosts can send a NO_VALID_HIP_TRANSPORT_MODE notification (error code 100) before closing the association.

One important constraint: the HIP base exchange and re-keying UPDATE messages (which create or change encryption keys) MUST NOT be sent over any encrypted connection, including those using these transport modes. This prevents bootstrapping problems where you would need the new keys to send the message that creates them.
sections.eli5: The two hosts negotiate which mode to use, checking that both agree. If they don't agree, they keep talking the old way. The agreement is signed so nobody can trick them into picking an unsafe mode.

sections.title: Connection Handling and Mobility
sections.content:
When using ESP or ESP-TCP modes, hosts must continue to accept HIP messages sent outside the encrypted connection (using the original unencrypted method) because the encrypted connection might fail. If the encrypted signaling connection fails, hosts renegotiate using unencrypted messages and re-establish the encrypted connection through a new mode negotiation.

For ESP-TCP mode, if the TCP connection fails to establish or breaks later, the host that initiated the mode negotiation should try again without proposing ESP-TCP. If local policy requires ESP-TCP and no fallback is allowed, the HIP association should be closed. The UPDATE or CLOSE message used for recovery must be sent using the same transport that was active when the negotiation started.

Host mobility and multihoming introduce additional complexity. When using ESP mode, the first mobility UPDATE message (which notifies the peer of a new address) SHOULD be sent using the old Security Association (SA), and subsequent messages use the new SAs. For ESP-TCP mode, the TCP connection moves to the new SA pair like any TCP connection would, but the initial mobility UPDATE messages SHOULD be sent over plain ESP rather than TCP, allowing hosts to detect address changes even if TCP is unreachable.
sections.eli5: If the encrypted tunnel breaks, the computers can still send unencrypted messages to rebuild it. When a computer moves to a new address, it carefully coordi nates the switchover using the old tunnel first, then the new one.

sections.title: Security and Confidentiality
sections.content:
By encrypting signaling messages over the ESP connection, all HIP control data (except the base exchange and re-keying messages) is protected from eavesdropping. The level of protection depends on the ESP encryption transform negotiated; NULL encryption provides no confidentiality, while other algorithms like AES provide strong encryption.

The mode negotiation itself is protected against downgrade attacks because the HIP_TRANSPORT_MODE parameter is signed as part of the base exchange or UPDATE packet. An attacker cannot change the modes listed in the parameter without breaking the packet's signature, which would cause the base exchange or update to fail. The only realistic downgrade attack is if both hosts accept the DEFAULT (unencrypted) mode; if either host's policy requires a secure mode, the base exchange or update simply fails.

A host requiring confidentiality for signaling must verify that encryption is actually negotiated on the ESP connection, not just that the mode is set, since NULL encryption is technically valid. Additionally, when HIP messages are encrypted, on-path network elements like firewalls and HIP-aware NATs cannot see HIP headers or unencrypted parameters unless they have the encryption keys. This contrasts with the original HIP design, which deliberately exposed some information to HIP-aware NATs. If encrypted signaling is used, only the unencrypted base exchange and initial UPDATEs are visible to such intermediaries.
sections.eli5: The tunnel hides the control messages from eavesdroppers. The agreement about which tunnel to use is sealed with signatures, so attackers cannot downgrade it to the unencrypted mode. But hosts must check that encryption is really happening, not just pretended.
